Plenary Verbal Inspiration
PLEE-nuh-ree VUR-buhl in-spuh-RAY-shuhn
noun
From plenary (full) + verbal (of the words) + inspiration (in-breathing); the doctrine that all the words of Scripture are God-breathed.

📖 Biblical Definition

Plenary verbal inspiration is the doctrine that the whole of Scripture (plenary, full), and the very words of Scripture (verbal), are inspired—breathed out by God. It holds that the Holy Ghost so moved and superintended the human authors that what they wrote, down to the words, is the word of God, true and without error in the original autographs, and authoritative in all it affirms. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, theopneustos, God-breathed; holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. The inspiration is plenary: it extends to all the Scripture, not merely to certain doctrines or moral teachings, but to history, prophecy, and every part. And it is verbal: it reaches to the words themselves, for the Lord and His apostles built arguments on single words and the very tenses of verbs. This does not make the human authors mere pens; the Spirit used their minds, styles, and circumstances, yet so governed them that the result is wholly the word of God and wholly their word, without error. The dictionary honors plenary verbal inspiration as the church’s confession of the nature of Scripture, the foundation of its authority and sufficiency, against every doctrine that would make the Bible merely contain the word of God, or err in its words, or inspire only its religious sentiments. The Scripture cannot be broken, for it is the very breath of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that all Scripture, down to its words, is breathed out by God—true, without error, and authoritative—the holy authors moved by the Holy Ghost.

📖 Key Scripture

2Ti 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

2Pe 1:21 — "For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost."

Mat 5:18 — "For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

Joh 10:35 — "If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Inspiration is reduced to the Bible merely containing God’s word, or inspiring only its sentiments; Scripture testifies that its very words are breathed out by God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the liberal-critical reduction. The chief corruption, flowing from modern liberal and critical scholarship, denies plenary verbal inspiration in various ways: that the Bible merely contains the word of God amid human error; that only its religious or moral teachings are inspired, not its history or its words; that inspiration means only an elevated human insight, not the breathing-out of God. Each of these makes the church, the scholar, or the reader the judge of which words are God’s, and so dissolves the authority of Scripture into the authority of man.

The principle to recover is the Bible’s own testimony to itself. All scripture is given by inspiration of God—theopneustos, God-breathed (2 Tim 3:16); the prophecy came not by the will of man, but holy men spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost (2 Pet 1:21). The Lord pressed inspiration down to the jot and tittle, the smallest stroke of the law (Matt 5:18), and declared that the scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). This is plenary—the whole—and verbal—the very words. To confess it is to bow before the Bible as the very breath of God, true, authoritative, and sufficient; to deny it is to set up a Bible within the Bible, judged by the spirit of the age.

Plenary (full) + verbal (of the words) + inspiration (God-breathing); the doctrine that all the words of Scripture are breathed out by God, true and authoritative.
